title: Congo Starts Ebola Shots for Health Workers in Outbreak's Center
summary: In a city called Bunia, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, health workers rolled up their sleeves on Saturday. They were getting vaccinated against Ebola — a dangerous virus that causes fever and bleeding. This outbreak is the fastest-growing and deadliest of all 17 Ebola outbreaks Congo has ever had. The workers are first in line because they treat sick patients every day. 'Our collective duty is to protect life,' said Maj. Gen. Gaby Kasongo Mulumba, the military governor of Ituri province. 'These workers are particularly exposed and deeply involved in the response.' The shot is called Ervebo. It worked in past outbreaks caused by a different Ebola type — the Zaire strain. This outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved vaccine or treatment. Scientists are studying whether Ervebo can protect against it too, because the two viruses are related. The plan is to vaccinate 20,000 front-line workers over six to nine months in Ituri and North Kivu. The World Health Organization approved 70,000 doses. About 50,000 are for health workers, and 20,000 are for a clinical trial — a medical study — to see if the vaccine works against Bundibugyo. As of Saturday, Congo had 7,541 confirmed cases, 3,639 deaths, and 1,823 people who recovered. Dr. Jeannot Elua said the vaccine is 'beneficial.' 'We healthcare workers don't really have a choice,' he said.
why_it_matters: Outbreaks stop when people notice symptoms early and get help fast, so learning how vaccines and health workers protect a community shows you how diseases are contained.

background_read: Ebola is a dangerous virus that was first found in 1976 in the Democratic Republic of Congo, near a river called the Ebola River.
The World Health Organization (a United Nations group that helps countries fight disease) checks vaccines and sends medicines and teams to outbreaks.
The Ervebo vaccine was used to protect people in earlier Congo outbreaks caused by the Zaire strain, which is closely related to the Bundibugyo virus.

WHERE: Bunia in Ituri province, with plans also for North Kivu, using 70,000 doses approved by the World Health Organization.
WHY: This is the fastest-growing and deadliest of Congo's 17 Ebola outbreaks, caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved vaccine or treatment.
